notes: **Alo is only used on the phone.** In person, it's *merhaba*. Saying who you are with *ben ...* at the start of a phone call is an almost compulsory Turkish habit.

**Rahatsız ediyor muyum?** — "am I disturbing you?" — is the polite way to open a call, and the answer is almost always *hiç de değil* or *estağfurullah* ("not at all"). These courtesies are expected, not just decoration.
**Getireyim mi?** uses the *-eyim* form, a close relative of *-elim* from unit 15: one for "let me", one for "let's". *Ne yapayım?* (what should I do?), *Gideyim mi?* (shall I go?).

**Arriving at a Turkish home empty-handed is considered a bit rude.** The usual gifts: *tatlı* (sweets), *çiçek* (flowers), or something for the hosts' children. The host will say no — and you should still bring it.

blocks.text: To say "I like swimming", Turkish first turns the verb into a noun, then gives it the object suffix: **stem + -me/-ma + -yi** — much like English *swim → swimming*.

Compare the pattern from unit 10: *yüzmek istiyorum* (I want to swim) uses the full dictionary form, while *yüzmeyi seviyorum* (I like swimming) uses the noun form. Different verbs demand different forms — so learn the partner together with the verb.

blocks.title: Hoşuma gidiyor
items: There's a second way to say "I like", and Turks use it as often as *sevmek*: *hoşuma gidiyor*, literally "it goes to my pleasure".
*Bu şarkı hoşuma gidiyor* (I like this song). *Sevmek* feels deeper and more lasting; *hoşuma gitmek* is lighter, about the impression in the moment.

blocks.text: There are two ways to say something needs to be done, and both are common.
The form: stem + *-me/-ma* + possessive suffix + *lazım*. The word *gerek* can replace *lazım* without changing the meaning.
*-meli* feels a little stronger and more written; *lazım* is more everyday. At A1, master one of them well — and understand the other when you hear it.

blocks.title: Visiting a Turkish home
items: Shoes come off at the door — almost always, and the host will offer slippers. Tea will arrive without your asking, and your second glass will be filled without a question.
Turning food down once counts as good manners, not refusal; the host will offer again. If you really are full: *Çok tokum, gerçekten* — "I'm really full".
